newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF says Bulgaria likely to win funding by year end.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Bulgaria likely to win funding by year end.

text.p: Bulgaria is likely to reach a funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) by the end of 1996 if a proposal for a currency board receives strong political support, an IMF official said on Tuesday.

"There is a realistic prospect for coming to an arrangement by the turn of the year if this idea (currency board) meets strong public support and if we agree on all the policies that need to go with it," the deputy director of the IMF European department, Michael Deppler, told reporters.
An IMF team headed by Deppler has met government officials, politicians and bankers in the past 10 days to discuss introducing a currency board to curb inflation and restore confidence in the lev.

"We are very encouraged by the developments of the past week. I think there is new awareness in Bulgaria about the way it goes about its financial business," said Deppler on departure from the Sofia airport.
Other members of the IMF mission will remain in Sofia until Thursday to develop a work plan for more specialised missions to follow shortly, said an IMF statement.
Under the currency board system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves.
Currency boards usually peg the local currency to the dollar. Argentina, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia have all used currency boards to restore confidence and defeat hyperinflation.

Under the proposal, the central bank would be split into the currency board, which will be reponsible for the issuance of the lev and foreign exchange, and a banking department that will be responsible for banking supervision.
On Monday, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov and Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said they supported introduction of a currency board as the only way to stabilise the economy.
Videnov said a currency board would prevent the central bank from pouring money into refinancing of collapsing banks or fuelling inflation by printing money.
Implementation would have to be approved by parliament, in which Videnov's Socialist party has a majority.
But the central bank has written to Videnov and other senior officials to suggest setting up a group of international experts to evaluate alternatives to the IMF's proposed currency board.
The IMF has not said how much support it would provide if a currency board plan was adopted but urged the government to draft the 1997 budget focusing on the requirements of the currency board.

The IMF has twice postponed a $115 million loan due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
